questions.question: Find $x$ and $y$ if $(2x,\ x+y)=(6,\ 2)$.
questions.answer:
**$x=3,\ y=-1$**

Two matrices (here row matrices) are equal only when their corresponding entries are equal. Comparing entry by entry:

$$2x=6\ \Rightarrow\ x=3$$

$$x+y=2\ \Rightarrow\ 3+y=2\ \Rightarrow\ y=-1$$

$$\therefore\ x=3,\quad y=-1$$

**Check:** $(2\times3,\ 3+(-1))=(6,\ 2)$ ✓. The error to avoid is forgetting that $y$ depends on the value of $x$ found first — substituting $x=3$ gives $y=-1$, not $y=2-3=1$.

questions.question: A bag contains 3 white and 2 black balls. Find the probability of drawing a white ball at random.
questions.answer:
**$\dfrac{3}{5}$**

The total number of balls is

$$n(S)=3+2=5$$

Each ball is equally likely, so the sample space has 5 equally likely outcomes. The favourable outcomes are the 3 white balls:

$$n(E)=3$$

$$P(\text{white})=\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}=\frac{3}{5}$$

(Note the answer must lie between 0 and 1 — the option $\frac32$ is impossible for any probability, which rules it out immediately.)

questions.question: Evaluate: $\displaystyle\int\frac{1}{x^2}\,dx$
questions.answer:
**$-\dfrac{1}{x}+c$**

Write the integrand as a power, $\dfrac{1}{x^2}=x^{-2}$, and apply the power rule with $n=-2$:

$$\int x^{-2}dx=\frac{x^{-2+1}}{-2+1}+c=\frac{x^{-1}}{-1}+c=-\frac{1}{x}+c$$

**Check:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-\dfrac1x\right)=-\dfrac{d}{dx}x^{-1}=-(-1)x^{-2}=\dfrac{1}{x^2}$ ✓.

The power rule fails only at $n=-1$, where the integral is $\log x$ — that is why option (iv) is a distractor.

questions.question: Prove that $\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$.
questions.answer:
**$\dfrac{\pi}{2}$**

Let $\sin^{-1}x=\theta$, where $x\in[-1,1]$ and $\theta\in\left[-\dfrac{\pi}{2},\dfrac{\pi}{2}\right]$. Then

$$\sin\theta=x$$

Now use the co-function identity $\cos\left(\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta\right)=\sin\theta=x$. Since $\theta$ lies in $\left[-\frac{\pi}{2},\frac{\pi}{2}\right]$, the angle $\dfrac{\pi}{2}-\theta$ lies in $[0,\pi]$, which is exactly the range of $\cos^{-1}$. Therefore

$$\cos^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta$$

Adding $\theta=\sin^{-1}x$ to both sides:

$$\sin^{-1}x+\cos^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}\qquad\blacksquare$$

The range conditions matter: without them we could not conclude $\cos^{-1}x=\frac{\pi}{2}-\theta$, because $\cos^{-1}$ returns a value in $[0,\pi]$ only.

questions.topic: Powers of i — Complex Numbers (old-syllabus item)
questions.question: Evaluate: $i^{35}$
questions.answer:
**$-i$**

Use $i^2=-1$ and the fact that the powers of $i$ repeat with period 4:

$$i^1=i,\quad i^2=-1,\quad i^3=-i,\quad i^4=1$$

Divide the exponent by 4: $35=4\times8+3$, so

$$i^{35}=i^{4\times8+3}=\left(i^4\right)^{8}\cdot i^3=1^{8}\cdot i^3=i^3=-i$$

So $i^{35}=-i$.

**Careful:** $i^3=i^2\cdot i=(-1)i=-i$, not $i$. With that correction the answer is $-i$ (option (ii) in the printed paper).

questions.question: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}2&7\\9&8\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}1&2\\0&3\end{bmatrix}$, then find $A-B$.
questions.answer:
**$\begin{bmatrix}1&5\\9&5\end{bmatrix}$**

Subtract corresponding entries:

$$A-B=\begin{bmatrix}2-1 & 7-2\\ 9-0 & 8-3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}1&5\\9&5\end{bmatrix}$$

Addition and subtraction are defined only for matrices of the **same order**; here both are $2\times2$, so the operation is legitimate entry by entry. (Option (iii) is $A+B$, a common slip.)

questions.question: If $y=\sin(\cot x)$, then find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$.
questions.answer:
**$-\cos(\cot x)\cdot\mathrm{cosec}^2x$**

Apply the chain rule with $y=\sin u$ and $u=\cot x$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\cos u\cdot\frac{du}{dx}=\cos(\cot x)\cdot\frac{d}{dx}(\cot x)$$

Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}(\cot x)=-\mathrm{cosec}^2x$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=-\cos(\cot x)\,\mathrm{cosec}^2x$$

The negative sign is essential: $\cot x$ decreases on $(0,\pi)$, so the sine of it decreases too, making the derivative negative wherever $\cos(\cot x)>0$.

questions.question: Solve: $y\,dx-x\,dy=xydx$.
questions.answer:
**$y=xe^{-x}+c$ *(the printed key writes $y=xe^{-x}$, absorbing the constant)***

Bring the $dx$ terms together:

$$y\,dx-x\,dy=xy\,dx\ \Rightarrow\ -x\,dy=xy\,dx-y\,dx=y(x-1)dx$$

$$\frac{dy}{y}=\frac{(1-x)}{x}\,dx=\left(\frac1x-1\right)dx$$

Integrate both sides:

$$\log y=\log x-x+c$$

$$\log y-\log x=-x+c\ \Rightarrow\ \log\frac{y}{x}=-x+c$$

$$\frac{y}{x}=e^{-x}\cdot e^{c}=Ae^{-x}$$

$$\therefore\ y=Axe^{-x}$$

Writing the arbitrary constant as $A=e^{c}$ (and taking $A=1$ if the constant is absorbed on the other side) gives the printed form $y=xe^{-x}$. In general the solution is the one-parameter family $y=Axe^{-x}$.

questions.question: Evaluate: $\begin{vmatrix}4&9&7\\3&5&7\\5&4&5\end{vmatrix}$
questions.answer:
**77**

Expand along the first row using $|A|=a_{11}C_{11}+a_{12}C_{12}+a_{13}C_{13}$:

$$=4\begin{vmatrix}5&7\\4&5\end{vmatrix}-9\begin{vmatrix}3&7\\5&5\end{vmatrix}+7\begin{vmatrix}3&5\\5&4\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=4(25-28)-9(15-35)+7(12-25)$$

$$=4(-3)-9(-20)+7(-13)$$

$$=-12+180-91=77$$

$$\therefore\ \begin{vmatrix}4&9&7\\3&5&7\\5&4&5\end{vmatrix}=77$$

The middle cofactor carries a **minus** sign — dropping it gives $-12-180-91$, a very different number.

questions.question: Prove that the vectors $\hat i-2\hat j+5\hat k$ and $-2\hat i+4\hat j+2\hat k$ are mutually perpendicular.
questions.answer:
**$\vec a\cdot\vec b=0$**

Two non-zero vectors are perpendicular exactly when their dot product is zero. With $\vec a=\hat i-2\hat j+5\hat k$ and $\vec b=-2\hat i+4\hat j+2\hat k$:

$$\vec a\cdot\vec b=(1)(-2)+(-2)(4)+(5)(2)=-2-8+10=0$$

$$\therefore\ \vec a\cdot\vec b=0\ \Rightarrow\ \vec a\perp\vec b\qquad\blacksquare$$

(Compare the cross product, which is $\vec a\times\vec b=0$ only for *parallel* vectors — the opposite condition.)

questions.question: If $f(x)=4x^2-5x$, find the value of $\dfrac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}$.
questions.answer:
Substitute $x+h$ into the function:

$$f(x+h)=4(x+h)^2-5(x+h)$$

$$=4\left(x^2+2xh+h^2\right)-5x-5h$$

$$=4x^2+8xh+4h^2-5x-5h$$

Now subtract $f(x)=4x^2-5x$:

$$f(x+h)-f(x)=\left(4x^2+8xh+4h^2-5x-5h\right)-\left(4x^2-5x\right)$$

$$=8xh+4h^2-5h$$

$$=h(8x+4h-5)$$

Divide by $h$ (valid for $h\ne0$):

$$\frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}=\frac{h(8x+4h-5)}{h}=8x+4h-5$$

$$\therefore\ \frac{f(x+h)-f(x)}{h}=8x+4h-5$$

Letting $h\to0$ gives $f'(x)=8x-5$, which agrees with differentiating $4x^2-5x$ directly — a useful check on the algebra.

questions.question: Prove that $2\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{5}+\tan^{-1}\dfrac{1}{4}=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{32}{43}$.
questions.answer:
Group the doubled term first, using $2\tan^{-1}x=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{2x}{1-x^2}$ (valid for $|x|<1$):

$$2\tan^{-1}\frac15=\tan^{-1}\frac{2\cdot\frac15}{1-\frac{1}{25}}=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac25}{\frac{24}{25}}=\tan^{-1}\frac{2}{5}\cdot\frac{25}{24}=\tan^{-1}\frac{5}{12}$$

Now combine with $\tan^{-1}\dfrac14$ using $\tan^{-1}x+\tan^{-1}y=\tan^{-1}\dfrac{x+y}{1-xy}$:

$$\tan^{-1}\frac{5}{12}+\tan^{-1}\frac{1}{4}=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac{5}{12}+\frac14}{1-\frac{5}{12}\cdot\frac14}$$

$$=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac{5+3}{12}}{\frac{48-5}{48}}=\tan^{-1}\frac{\frac{8}{12}}{\frac{43}{48}}=\tan^{-1}\left(\frac23\cdot\frac{48}{43}\right)=\tan^{-1}\frac{32}{43}$$

$$\therefore\ 2\tan^{-1}\frac15+\tan^{-1}\frac14=\tan^{-1}\frac{32}{43}\qquad\blacksquare$$

**Check numerically:** $2\tan^{-1}0.2+\tan^{-1}0.25=0.6397698$ rad and $\tan^{-1}\frac{32}{43}=0.6397698$ rad ✓. Since $\frac{32}{43}<1$, the combined angle is acute and the principal value is the one obtained.

questions.question: Find $\dfrac{dy}{dx}$ if $y=\dfrac{1-\cos x}{1+\cos x}$.
questions.answer:
Apply the quotient rule $\left(\dfrac uv\right)'=\dfrac{u'v-uv'}{v^2}$ with $u=1-\cos x$ and $v=1+\cos x$, so $u'=\sin x$ and $v'=-\sin x$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{\sin x(1+\cos x)-(1-\cos x)(-\sin x)}{(1+\cos x)^2}$$

$$=\frac{\sin x+\sin x\cos x+\sin x-\sin x\cos x}{(1+\cos x)^2}$$

$$=\frac{2\sin x}{(1+\cos x)^2}$$

So

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{2\sin x}{(1+\cos x)^2}$$

**Equivalent half-angle form.** Using $1+\cos x=2\cos^2\dfrac x2$ and $\sin x=2\sin\dfrac x2\cos\dfrac x2$:

$$\frac{dy}{dx}=\frac{4\sin\frac x2\cos\frac x2}{4\cos^4\frac x2}=\frac{\sin\frac x2}{\cos^3\frac x2}=\tan\frac x2\sec^2\frac x2$$

$$\text{Since }\frac{d}{dx}\tan\frac x2=\frac12\sec^2\frac x2\text{, this says }\frac{dy}{dx}=2\cdot\frac12\sec^2\frac x2\tan\frac x2=\frac{d}{dx}\left(2\tan\frac x2\right)\text{ — and indeed }\frac{1-\cos x}{1+\cos x}=\tan^2\frac x2.$$

So a slicker route is $y=\tan^2\dfrac x2$, giving $\dfrac{dy}{dx}=2\tan\dfrac x2\cdot\dfrac12\sec^2\dfrac x2=\tan\dfrac x2\sec^2\dfrac x2$, the same result.

questions.question: Factorize: $\begin{vmatrix}a-b-c & 2a & 2a\\ 2b & b-c-a & 2b\\ 2c & 2c & c-a-b\end{vmatrix}$
questions.answer:
Take the determinant

$$\Delta=\begin{vmatrix}a-b-c&2a&2a\\2b&b-c-a&2b\\2c&2c&c-a-b\end{vmatrix}$$

**Step 1 — column operation $C_1\to C_1-C_2$:**

$$C_1=\begin{pmatrix}(a-b-c)-2a\\ 2b-(b-c-a)\\ 2c-2c\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}-(a+b+c)\\ a+b+c\\ 0\end{pmatrix}=(a+b+c)\begin{pmatrix}-1\\1\\0\end{pmatrix}$$

**Step 2 — column operation $C_2\to C_2-C_3$:**

$$C_2=\begin{pmatrix}2a-2a\\ (b-c-a)-2b\\ 2c-(c-a-b)\end{pmatrix}=\begin{pmatrix}0\\ -(a+b+c)\\ a+b+c\end{pmatrix}=(a+b+c)\begin{pmatrix}0\\-1\\1\end{pmatrix}$$

Both operations leave the value of the determinant unchanged, so

$$\Delta=(a+b+c)^2\begin{vmatrix}-1&0&2a\\1&-1&2b\\0&1&c-a-b\end{vmatrix}$$

**Step 3 — expand the reduced determinant** along the first column:

$$\begin{vmatrix}-1&0&2a\\1&-1&2b\\0&1&c-a-b\end{vmatrix}=(-1)\begin{vmatrix}-1&2b\\1&c-a-b\end{vmatrix}-1\begin{vmatrix}0&2a\\1&c-a-b\end{vmatrix}+0$$

$$=(-1)\left[(-1)(c-a-b)-2b\right]-1\left[0-2a\right]$$

$$=(-1)\left[-c+a+b-2b\right]+2a$$

$$=(-1)\left[-c+a-b\right]+2a=c-a+b+2a=a+b+c$$

$$\therefore\ \Delta=(a+b+c)^2\cdot(a+b+c)$$

$$\therefore\ \begin{vmatrix}a-b-c&2a&2a\\2b&b-c-a&2b\\2c&2c&c-a-b\end{vmatrix}=(a+b+c)^3$$

**Check:** with $a=b=c=1$ the determinant is $\begin{vmatrix}-1&2&2\\2&-1&2\\2&2&-1\end{vmatrix}=-1(1-4)-2(-2-4)+2(4+2)=3+12+12=27=3^3$ ✓, and the reduced determinant equals $a+b+c=3$, as required.

questions.question: Test the continuity of the function $f(x)$ at $x=0$, where $f(x)=\dfrac{\sin x}{x}$ when $x\ne0$, and $f(x)=2$ when $x=0$.
questions.answer:
For continuity at $x=0$ we need the left-hand limit, the right-hand limit and the value $f(0)$ all to exist and be equal.

**Value at the point:**

$$f(0)=2$$

**Right-hand limit** ($x\to0^+$, i.e. $x=0+h$ with $h\to0^+$):

$$\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\sin(0+h)}{0+h}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\sin h}{h}=1$$

**Left-hand limit** ($x\to0^-$, i.e. $x=0-h$):

$$\lim_{x\to0^-}f(x)=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\sin(0-h)}{0-h}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{-\sin h}{-h}=\lim_{h\to0}\frac{\sin h}{h}=1$$

So

$$\lim_{x\to0^+}f(x)=\lim_{x\to0^-}f(x)=1\quad\text{but}\quad f(0)=2$$

$$\lim_{x\to0}f(x)=1\ne f(0)$$

$$\therefore\ f(x)\ \text{is \textbf{not continuous} at }x=0$$

This is a **removable discontinuity**: the function would become continuous at $0$ if the value were redefined as $f(0)=1$. (The printed key states 'continuous when…' but its own working shows the limits equal 1 while $f(0)=2$; the correct conclusion is discontinuity.)

questions.question: Find the acute angle between two lines that have the direction ratios $(1,1,0)$ and $(2,1,2)$.
questions.answer:
The angle between two lines is the angle between their direction vectors. With $\vec b_1=(1,1,0)$ and $\vec b_2=(2,1,2)$:

$$\cos\theta=\frac{\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2}{|\vec b_1||\vec b_2|}$$

$$\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2=(1)(2)+(1)(1)+(0)(2)=3$$

$$|\vec b_1|=\sqrt{1^2+1^2+0^2}=\sqrt2,\qquad |\vec b_2|=\sqrt{2^2+1^2+2^2}=\sqrt9=3$$

$$\cos\theta=\frac{3}{\sqrt2\cdot3}=\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$$

$$\therefore\ \theta=45^\circ=\frac{\pi}{4}$$

Since $\cos\theta>0$, the angle obtained is already the **acute** angle. (Had the dot product been negative, $\theta$ would be obtuse and the acute angle would be $180^\circ-\theta$.)

questions.question: Evaluate any one: (i) $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{1+\cos 2x}$ (ii) $\displaystyle\int\tan^4x\,dx$.
questions.answer:
**(i) $\displaystyle\int\frac{dx}{1+\cos2x}$.** Use $1+\cos2x=2\cos^2x$:

$$I=\int\frac{dx}{2\cos^2x}=\frac12\int\sec^2x\,dx$$

$$=\frac12\tan x+c$$

$$\therefore\ \int\frac{dx}{1+\cos2x}=\frac12\tan x+c$$

**Check:** $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(\dfrac12\tan x\right)=\dfrac12\sec^2x=\dfrac{1}{2\cos^2x}=\dfrac{1}{1+\cos2x}$ ✓.

**(ii) $\displaystyle\int\tan^4x\,dx$.** Write $\tan^4x=\tan^2x\cdot\tan^2x=\tan^2x\left(\sec^2x-1\right)=\tan^2x\sec^2x-\tan^2x$, and split:

$$\int\tan^4x\,dx=\int\tan^2x\sec^2x\,dx-\int\tan^2x\,dx$$

For the first integral put $t=\tan x$, $dt=\sec^2x\,dx$:

$$\int\tan^2x\sec^2x\,dx=\int t^2dt=\frac{t^3}{3}=\frac{\tan^3x}{3}$$

For the second, use $\tan^2x=\sec^2x-1$:

$$\int\tan^2x\,dx=\int\left(\sec^2x-1\right)dx=\tan x-x$$

Therefore

$$\int\tan^4x\,dx=\frac{\tan^3x}{3}-\tan x+x+c$$

$$\therefore\ \int\tan^4x\,dx=\frac{\tan^3x}{3}-\tan x+x+c$$

**Check by differentiating:** $\tan^2x\sec^2x-\sec^2x+1=\tan^2x\sec^2x-\tan^2x=\tan^2x(\sec^2x-1)=\tan^4x$ ✓.

questions.question: Evaluate any one: (i) $\displaystyle\int_0^1\sqrt{\frac{1-x}{1+x}}\,dx$ (ii) $\displaystyle\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\frac{1-\sin x}{1-\cos x}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
**(i) $\displaystyle I=\int_0^1\sqrt{\frac{1-x}{1+x}}\,dx$.** Put $x=\cos2\theta$, so $dx=-2\sin2\theta\,d\theta$. Limits: $x=0\Rightarrow\cos2\theta=0\Rightarrow\theta=\frac{\pi}{4}$; $x=1\Rightarrow\cos2\theta=1\Rightarrow\theta=0$.

Then

$$\sqrt{\frac{1-x}{1+x}}=\sqrt{\frac{1-\cos2\theta}{1+\cos2\theta}}=\sqrt{\frac{2\sin^2\theta}{2\cos^2\theta}}=\tan\theta$$

$$I=\int_{\pi/4}^{0}\tan\theta\,(-2\sin2\theta)\,d\theta=2\int_0^{\pi/4}\tan\theta\sin2\theta\,d\theta$$

With $\sin2\theta=2\sin\theta\cos\theta$:

$$I=2\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{\sin\theta}{\cos\theta}\cdot2\sin\theta\cos\theta\,d\theta=4\int_0^{\pi/4}\sin^2\theta\,d\theta$$

$$=4\int_0^{\pi/4}\frac{1-\cos2\theta}{2}d\theta=2\left[\theta-\frac{\sin2\theta}{2}\right]_0^{\pi/4}$$

$$=2\left[\left(\frac{\pi}{4}-\frac12\right)-0\right]=\frac{\pi}{2}-1$$

$$\therefore\ \int_0^1\sqrt{\frac{1-x}{1+x}}\,dx=\frac{\pi}{2}-1\approx0.5708$$

**(ii) $\displaystyle J=\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\frac{1-\sin x}{1-\cos x}\,dx$.** Use the half-angle forms $1-\cos x=2\sin^2\dfrac x2$ and $\sin x=2\sin\dfrac x2\cos\dfrac x2$:

$$\frac{1-\sin x}{1-\cos x}=\frac{1-2\sin\frac x2\cos\frac x2}{2\sin^2\frac x2}=\frac{1}{2}\mathrm{cosec}^2\frac x2-\cot\frac x2$$

$$J=\int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\left[\frac12\mathrm{cosec}^2\frac x2-\cot\frac x2\right]dx$$

Since $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-\cot\dfrac x2\right)=\dfrac12\mathrm{cosec}^2\dfrac x2$ and $\dfrac{d}{dx}\left(-2\log\sin\dfrac x2\right)=-\cot\dfrac x2$:

$$J=\left[-\cot\frac x2-2\log\sin\frac x2\right]_{\pi/2}^{\pi}$$

At $x=\pi$: $-\cot\dfrac{\pi}{2}-2\log\sin\dfrac{\pi}{2}=0-2\log1=0$.

At $x=\dfrac{\pi}{2}$: $-\cot\dfrac{\pi}{4}-2\log\sin\dfrac{\pi}{4}=-1-2\log\dfrac{1}{\sqrt2}=-1+\log2$.

$$J=0-\left(-1+\log2\right)=1-\log2$$

$$\therefore\ \int_{\pi/2}^{\pi}\frac{1-\sin x}{1-\cos x}\,dx=1-\log2\approx0.3069$$

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet's working for (ii) is correct through $-\cot\frac x2-2\log\sin\frac x2$ but the final evaluation collects the boundary terms as $1+2\log\frac{1}{\sqrt2}=1-\log2$ while printing the intermediate as $2\log\frac{1}{\sqrt2}$, i.e. it writes $1-\log2$ only after a sign slip in the log coefficient; the value $1-\log2$ it prints is nevertheless the correct one. For (i) the key prints $\frac{\pi}{\sqrt2}-1$; the correct value is $\frac{\pi}{2}-1$ (numerically 0.5708, confirmed).

questions.question: Evaluate any one: (i) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^3x}{\sin^3x+\cos^3x}\,dx$ (ii) $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\frac{x}{1+\sin x}\,dx$.
questions.answer:
**(i) $\displaystyle I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^3x}{\sin^3x+\cos^3x}dx$.** Use the property $\displaystyle\int_0^{a}f(x)dx=\int_0^{a}f(a-x)dx$ with $a=\frac{\pi}{2}$, exchanging $\sin$ and $\cos$:

$$I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\cos^3x}{\cos^3x+\sin^3x}dx$$

Add the two expressions for $I$:

$$2I=\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^3x+\cos^3x}{\sin^3x+\cos^3x}dx=\int_0^{\pi/2}1\,dx=\frac{\pi}{2}$$

$$\therefore\ I=\frac{\pi}{4}$$

**So $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi/2}\frac{\sin^3x}{\sin^3x+\cos^3x}dx=\frac{\pi}{4}\approx0.7854$** (verified numerically), and the method works for any exponent: the answer is always $\frac{\pi}{4}$ because the integrand and its $\frac{\pi}{2}$-reflection add to 1.

**(ii) $\displaystyle J=\int_0^{\pi}\frac{x}{1+\sin x}dx$.** Apply the same property with $a=\pi$:

$$J=\int_0^{\pi}\frac{\pi-x}{1+\sin(\pi-x)}dx=\int_0^{\pi}\frac{\pi-x}{1+\sin x}dx$$

Adding:

$$2J=\int_0^{\pi}\frac{x+(\pi-x)}{1+\sin x}dx=\pi\int_0^{\pi}\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}$$

Now $\dfrac{1}{1+\sin x}=\dfrac{1-\sin x}{1-\sin^2x}=\dfrac{1-\sin x}{\cos^2x}=\sec^2x-\sec x\tan x$, so

$$\int\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}=\tan x-\sec x$$

$$\int_0^{\pi}\frac{dx}{1+\sin x}=\left[\tan x-\sec x\right]_0^{\pi}=\left[\tan\pi-\sec\pi\right]-\left[\tan0-\sec0\right]$$

$$=\left[0-(-1)\right]-\left[0-1\right]=1+1=2$$

$$2J=\pi(2)=2\pi\ \Rightarrow\ J=\pi$$

**So $\displaystyle\int_0^{\pi}\frac{x}{1+\sin x}dx=\pi\approx3.1416$** (verified numerically).

The slight delicacy is that $\tan x-\sec x$ has a singularity at $x=\frac{\pi}{2}$ inside the interval; taking the limit on each side shows the improper integral converges to 2, which is why the direct substitution still gives the right answer.

questions.question: If $\vec a=2\hat i-3\hat j-5\hat k$ and $\vec b=-7\hat i+6\hat j+8\hat k$, find $\vec a\times\vec b$.
questions.answer:
Write the cross product as a determinant with the unit vectors in the first row:

$$\vec a\times\vec b=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ 2&-3&-5\\ -7&6&8\end{vmatrix}$$

Expand along the first row:

$$=\hat i\begin{vmatrix}-3&-5\\ 6&8\end{vmatrix}-\hat j\begin{vmatrix}2&-5\\ -7&8\end{vmatrix}+\hat k\begin{vmatrix}2&-3\\ -7&6\end{vmatrix}$$

$$=\hat i\left[(-3)(8)-(-5)(6)\right]-\hat j\left[(2)(8)-(-5)(-7)\right]+\hat k\left[(2)(6)-(-3)(-7)\right]$$

$$=\hat i(-24+30)-\hat j(16-35)+\hat k(12-21)$$

$$=6\hat i+19\hat j-9\hat k$$

$$\therefore\ \vec a\times\vec b=6\hat i+19\hat j-9\hat k$$

**Check perpendicularity:** $\vec a\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=2(6)+(-3)(19)+(-5)(-9)=12-57+45=0$ ✓ and $\vec b\cdot(\vec a\times\vec b)=-42+114-72=0$ ✓, as the cross product must be.

questions.question: Find the equation of the plane perpendicular to the line joining the points (2,−1,2) and (3,2,−1), and passing through the point (4,−3,1).
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — direction of the line.** The direction ratios of the line joining $A(2,-1,2)$ and $B(3,2,-1)$ are

$$(3-2,\ 2-(-1),\ -1-2)=(1,\ 3,\ -3)$$

Since the plane is perpendicular to this line, this vector is a **normal** to the plane: $\vec n=(1,3,-3)$.

**Step 2 — point–normal form.** The equation of the plane through $(x_1,y_1,z_1)=(4,-3,1)$ with normal $(a,b,c)$ is

$$a(x-x_1)+b(y-y_1)+c(z-z_1)=0$$

$$1(x-4)+3(y+3)-3(z-1)=0$$

$$x-4+3y+9-3z+3=0$$

$$\therefore\ x+3y-3z+8=0$$

So the required plane is

$$x+3y-3z+8=0$$

**Check:** the point $(4,-3,1)$ satisfies $4+3(-3)-3(1)+8=4-9-3+8=0$ ✓, and the normal $(1,3,-3)$ is parallel to the direction $(1,3,-3)$ of $AB$ ✓.

questions.question: 10 coins are tossed. What is the probability that exactly 5 heads appear?
questions.answer:
Model the experiment as **binomial**: $n=10$ independent tosses, probability of a head

$$p=\frac12,\qquad q=1-p=\frac12$$

The probability of exactly $r$ successes is $P(r)={}^{n}C_r p^r q^{n-r}$. For $r=5$:

$$P(5)={}^{10}C_5\left(\frac12\right)^5\left(\frac12\right)^{5}={}^{10}C_5\left(\frac12\right)^{10}$$

$${}^{10}C_5=\frac{10!}{5!\,5!}=\frac{10\cdot9\cdot8\cdot7\cdot6}{5\cdot4\cdot3\cdot2\cdot1}=252$$

$$P(5)=\frac{252}{2^{10}}=\frac{252}{1024}=\frac{63}{256}$$

$$\therefore\ P(\text{exactly 5 heads})=\frac{63}{256}\approx0.2461$$

Since $p=q=\frac12$, the distribution is symmetric about $r=5$, and $\frac{63}{256}$ is the largest single term of the distribution.

questions.question: If $A=\begin{bmatrix}3&2\\7&5\end{bmatrix}$ and $B=\begin{bmatrix}6&7\\8&9\end{bmatrix}$, then show that $(AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — compute $AB$.**

$$AB=\begin{bmatrix}3&2\\7&5\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}6&7\\8&9\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}3(6)+2(8) & 3(7)+2(9)\\ 7(6)+5(8) & 7(7)+5(9)\end{bmatrix}$$

$$=\begin{bmatrix}18+16 & 21+18\\ 42+40 & 49+45\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}34&39\\82&94\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 2 — inverse of $AB$.** For a $2\times2$ matrix $\begin{bmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{bmatrix}$ the inverse is $\dfrac{1}{ad-bc}\begin{bmatrix}d&-b\\-c&a\end{bmatrix}$:

$$|AB|=(34)(94)-(39)(82)=3196-3198=-2$$

$$(AB)^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}\begin{bmatrix}94&-39\\-82&34\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-47 & \tfrac{39}{2}\\ 41 & -17\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 3 — the individual inverses.**

$$|A|=15-14=1,\qquad A^{-1}=\frac{1}{1}\begin{bmatrix}5&-2\\-7&3\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}5&-2\\-7&3\end{bmatrix}$$

$$|B|=54-56=-2,\qquad B^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}\begin{bmatrix}9&-7\\-8&6\end{bmatrix}=\begin{bmatrix}-\tfrac92 & \tfrac72\\ 4 & -3\end{bmatrix}$$

**Step 4 — multiply in the reversed order.**

$$B^{-1}A^{-1}=\frac{1}{-2}\begin{bmatrix}9&-7\\-8&6\end{bmatrix}\begin{bmatrix}5&-2\\-7&3\end{bmatrix}$$

$$=\frac{1}{-2}\begin{bmatrix}45+49 & -18-21\\ -40-42 & 16+18\end{bmatrix}=\frac{1}{-2}\begin{bmatrix}94&-39\\-82&34\end{bmatrix}$$

$$=\begin{bmatrix}-47 & \tfrac{39}{2}\\ 41 & -17\end{bmatrix}$$

$$\therefore\ (AB)^{-1}=B^{-1}A^{-1}=\begin{bmatrix}-47 & \tfrac{39}{2}\\ 41 & -17\end{bmatrix}\qquad\blacksquare$$

The **order reversal** is the whole point: matrix multiplication is not commutative, and $(AB)^{-1}$ must undo $B$ first, then $A$.

questions.question: Find the maximum and minimum values of the function $f(x)=2x^3-15x^2+36x+11$.
questions.answer:
**First derivative:**

$$f'(x)=6x^2-30x+36=6\left(x^2-5x+6\right)=6(x-2)(x-3)$$

**Stationary points:** $f'(x)=0$ gives

$$x=2\quad\text{or}\quad x=3$$

**Second derivative:**

$$f''(x)=12x-30$$

**Test:**

$$f''(2)=24-30=-6<0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local maximum at }x=2$$

$$f''(3)=36-30=6>0\ \Rightarrow\ \text{local minimum at }x=3$$

**Values:**

$$f(2)=2(8)-15(4)+36(2)+11=16-60+72+11=39$$

$$f(3)=2(27)-15(9)+36(3)+11=54-135+108+11=38$$

$$\therefore\ \text{maximum value }=39\ \text{at}\ x=2,\qquad \text{minimum value }=38\ \text{at}\ x=3$$

Since $f(x)\to-\infty$ as $x\to-\infty$ and $f(x)\to+\infty$ as $x\to+\infty$ (odd degree with positive leading coefficient), these are only local extrema; on the whole real line the function is unbounded. The printed key's values $39$ and $38$ are correct.

questions.question: Find the area of the region bounded by the parabola $y^2=4ax$, its axis and two ordinates $x=4$, $x=9$.
questions.answer:
The parabola $y^2=4ax$ (with $a>0$) opens along the positive $x$-axis, its vertex is at the origin and its axis is the $x$-axis ($y=0$). In the first quadrant

$$y=2\sqrt{ax}$$

The region asked for is bounded by the curve, the $x$-axis and the two vertical lines $x=4$ and $x=9$, so its area is

$$A=\int_4^9 2\sqrt{a}\,\sqrt{x}\,dx=2\sqrt a\int_4^9 x^{1/2}dx$$

$$=2\sqrt a\left[\frac{x^{3/2}}{3/2}\right]_4^9=\frac{4\sqrt a}{3}\left[x^{3/2}\right]_4^9$$

Since $9^{3/2}=27$ and $4^{3/2}=8$:

$$A=\frac{4\sqrt a}{3}(27-8)=\frac{4\sqrt a}{3}\times19$$

$$\therefore\ A=\frac{76\sqrt a}{3}\ \text{square units}$$

**For the usual case $a=1$** (i.e. $y^2=4x$) this gives $\dfrac{76}{3}\approx25.33$ square units, matching the printed key.

**Check by subtracting areas:** the area under $y=2\sqrt x$ from $0$ to $9$ is $\frac43(27)=36$, and from $0$ to $4$ it is $\frac43(8)=\frac{32}{3}$; the difference is $36-\frac{32}{3}=\frac{108-32}{3}=\frac{76}{3}$ ✓.

questions.question: Solve: $x\,dx+y\,dy=x\,dy-y\,dx$.
questions.answer:
Group the terms on each side:

$$x\,dx+y\,dy=x\,dy-y\,dx$$

The left-hand side is almost the differential of $x^2+y^2$, and the right-hand side is $x^2$ times the differential of $\dfrac yx$. The cleanest route is the **polar substitution**

$$x=r\cos\theta,\qquad y=r\sin\theta$$

Then

$$x^2+y^2=r^2,\qquad x\,dx+y\,dy=r\,dr$$

and, differentiating $\tan\theta=\dfrac yx$,

$$\sec^2\theta\,d\theta=\frac{x\,dy-y\,dx}{x^2}$$

$$\left(1+\tan^2\theta\right)d\theta=\frac{x\,dy-y\,dx}{x^2}$$

Multiplying by $x^2=r^2\cos^2\theta$ and using $1+\tan^2\theta=\sec^2\theta=\dfrac{1}{\cos^2\theta}$:

$$\frac{r^2\cos^2\theta}{\cos^2\theta}d\theta=x\,dy-y\,dx\ \Rightarrow\ r^2d\theta=x\,dy-y\,dx$$

Substituting both pieces into the differential equation:

$$r\,dr=r^2d\theta\ \Rightarrow\ \frac{dr}{r}=d\theta$$

Integrate:

$$\int\frac{dr}{r}=\int d\theta\ \Rightarrow\ \log r=\theta+c$$

Back-substitute $r=\sqrt{x^2+y^2}$ and $\theta=\tan^{-1}\dfrac yx$:

$$\log\sqrt{x^2+y^2}=\tan^{-1}\frac yx+c$$

$$\therefore\ \frac12\log\left(x^2+y^2\right)=\tan^{-1}\frac yx+c$$

or equivalently

$$\log\left(x^2+y^2\right)=2\tan^{-1}\frac yx+k,\qquad k=2c$$

which the key writes in exponential form as $x^2+y^2=e^{2\tan^{-1}(y/x)+k}$. The solution curves are the logarithmic spirals $r=Ae^{\theta}$.

questions.topic: Angle and Shortest Distance Between Lines
questions.question: Find the angle between the lines $\dfrac{5-x}{3}=\dfrac{y+3}{-4}=\dfrac{z-7}{0}$ and $\dfrac{x}{1}=\dfrac{1-y}{-2}=\dfrac{z-6}{2}$. / Or, find the shortest distance between the lines $\dfrac{x+3}{-4}=\dfrac{y-6}{3}=\dfrac{z}{2}$ and $\dfrac{x+2}{-4}=\dfrac{y}{1}=\dfrac{z-7}{1}$.
questions.answer:
**First part — angle between the lines.** Put each line into standard form $\dfrac{x-x_1}{a}=\dfrac{y-y_1}{b}=\dfrac{z-z_1}{c}$. Writing the first line as $\dfrac{x-5}{-3}=\dfrac{y+3}{-4}=\dfrac{z-7}{0}$ gives direction ratios

$$\vec b_1=(-3,-4,0)$$

and the second line $\dfrac{x-0}{1}=\dfrac{y-1}{2}=\dfrac{z-6}{2}$ (multiply $\dfrac{1-y}{-2}$ by $-1$ on both sides) gives

$$\vec b_2=(1,2,2)$$

$$\cos\theta=\frac{\vec b_1\cdot\vec b_2}{|\vec b_1||\vec b_2|}=\frac{(-3)(1)+(-4)(2)+(0)(2)}{\sqrt{9+16+0}\,\sqrt{1+4+4}}=\frac{-3-8}{5\cdot3}=\frac{-11}{15}$$

Since the cosine is negative, the angle between the direction vectors is obtuse; the **acute** angle between the lines satisfies

$$\cos\theta=\frac{11}{15}\ \Rightarrow\ \theta=\cos^{-1}\frac{11}{15}\approx42.8^\circ$$

*Note on the printed key:* the booklet takes the first direction as $(-3,-4,0)$ (correct) but then uses a vector $(-1,-2,2)$ in the dot product, obtaining $\cos\theta=\frac13$. With the directions as printed the correct value is $\left|\cos\theta\right|=\frac{11}{15}$, i.e. $\theta=\cos^{-1}\frac{11}{15}\approx42.8^\circ$.

**Or — shortest distance between the lines.**

$$L_1:\ \vec r=\vec a_1+t\vec b_1,\quad \vec a_1=(-3,6,0),\ \vec b_1=(-4,3,2)$$

$$L_2:\ \vec r=\vec a_2+s\vec b_2,\quad \vec a_2=(-2,0,7),\ \vec b_2=(-4,1,1)$$

$$\vec a_2-\vec a_1=(1,-6,7)$$

$$\vec b_1\times\vec b_2=\begin{vmatrix}\hat i&\hat j&\hat k\\ -4&3&2\\ -4&1&1\end{vmatrix}=\hat i(3-2)-\hat j(-4+8)+\hat k(-4+12)$$

$$=\hat i-4\hat j+8\hat k$$

$$\left|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\right|=\sqrt{1+16+64}=\sqrt{81}=9$$

$$d=\frac{\left|(\vec a_2-\vec a_1)\cdot(\vec b_1\times\vec b_2)\right|}{\left|\vec b_1\times\vec b_2\right|}=\frac{\left|(1)(1)+(-6)(-4)+(7)(8)\right|}{9}=\frac{1+24+56}{9}=\frac{81}{9}$$

$$\therefore\ d=9\ \text{units}$$

**The shortest distance is 9 units** — an unusually clean answer, which confirms the arithmetic.

questions.question: A coin is tossed 3 times. Find the probability that exactly 2 heads appear.
questions.answer:
The sample space consists of $2^3=8$ equally likely outcomes:

$$S=\{HHH,\ HHT,\ HTH,\ THH,\ HTT,\ THT,\ TTH,\ TTT\}$$

**By counting.** The event 'exactly 2 heads' is

$$E=\{HHT,\ HTH,\ THH\},\qquad n(E)=3$$

$$P(E)=\frac{n(E)}{n(S)}=\frac{3}{8}$$

**By the binomial distribution.** With $n=3$, $p=q=\frac12$ and $r=2$:

$$P(2)={}^{3}C_2\left(\frac12\right)^2\left(\frac12\right)^{1}=3\cdot\frac18=\frac38$$

$$\therefore\ P(\text{exactly 2 heads})=\frac{3}{8}=0.375$$

Either method gives $\frac38$; the binomial count ${}^{3}C_2=3$ simply counts the $\binom{3}{2}$ positions in which the two heads can occur.

questions.question: Solve the following L.P.P. graphically: Maximise $Z=5x+3y$ subject to $3x+5y\le15$, $5x+2y\le10$, $x,y\ge0$.
questions.answer:
**Step 1 — draw the boundary lines.**

$$3x+5y=15:\quad \text{intercepts }(5,0)\ \text{and}\ (0,3)$$

$$5x+2y=10:\quad \text{intercepts }(2,0)\ \text{and}\ (0,5)$$

Both inequalities are of the '$\le$' type and both are satisfied at the origin ($0\le15$, $0\le10$), so the feasible region is the intersection of the two origin-side half-planes together with the first quadrant. Its vertices are

$$O(0,0),\qquad A(2,0),\qquad C(0,3)$$

together with $B$, the intersection of the two lines.

**Step 2 — find $B$.** Solve

$$3x+5y=15\qquad\ldots(1)$$

$$5x+2y=10\qquad\ldots(2)$$

Multiply (1) by 5 and (2) by 3:

$$15x+25y=75,\qquad 15x+6y=30$$

Subtract:

$$19y=45\ \Rightarrow\ y=\frac{45}{19}$$

Substitute in (1): $3x=15-5\cdot\dfrac{45}{19}=15-\dfrac{225}{19}=\dfrac{285-225}{19}=\dfrac{60}{19}$, so

$$x=\frac{20}{19}$$

$$B=\left(\frac{20}{19},\ \frac{45}{19}\right)\approx(1.05,\ 2.37)$$

**Step 3 — evaluate $Z=5x+3y$ at the vertices.**

| Vertex | $Z=5x+3y$ |
|---|---|
| $O(0,0)$ | $0$ |
| $A(2,0)$ | $5(2)+3(0)=10$ |
| $B\left(\frac{20}{19},\frac{45}{19}\right)$ | $\frac{100}{19}+\frac{135}{19}=\frac{235}{19}=12\frac{7}{19}$ |
| $C(0,3)$ | $5(0)+3(3)=9$ |

**Step 4 — conclusion.** The largest value is

$$Z_{\max}=\frac{235}{19}=12\frac{7}{19}\approx12.37$$

attained at

$$x=\frac{20}{19},\qquad y=\frac{45}{19}$$

Notice that $C(0,3)$ gives $Z=9$ but the *feasible* corner at $x=0$ is $y=3$ only if it satisfies the second constraint: $5(0)+2(3)=6\le10$ ✓, so $C$ is indeed feasible; and $A(2,0)$ gives $3(2)+0=6\le15$ ✓. All four corners are feasible, and the objective is largest at $B$, the intersection point.
